reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An autosomal codominant disorder of the SERPINA1 gene, with the severe Z allele (PiZZ genotype) accounting for most clinically significant liver disease
The Z variant misfolds and polymerises within hepatocytes, so liver injury arises from toxic protein accumulation rather than from deficiency of circulating enzyme
It is a leading genetic cause of neonatal cholestasis and can also present as childhood or adult cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
Pulmonary disease results from a loss-of-function mechanism, with unopposed neutrophil elastase producing early-onset panacinar emphysema, especially in smokers
A low serum alpha-1-antitrypsin level with phenotype or genotype confirmation supports the diagnosis; note it is an acute-phase reactant that can be spuriously normal during inflammation
Liver biopsy shows diastase-resistant, PAS-positive globules within periportal hepatocytes representing retained polymerised protein
Hepatic management is supportive with surveillance for cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma and consideration of liver transplantation, which also corrects the metabolic defect
reference.pathophysiology: Alpha-1-antitrypsin is a serine protease inhibitor synthesised mainly in the liver that neutralises neutrophil elastase. The common pathogenic Z variant of SERPINA1 causes the protein to misfold and polymerise inside the endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes rather than being secreted. Two distinct problems follow: retention of the abnormal polymer is directly toxic to hepatocytes and drives cholestasis, fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, while the resulting low circulating enzyme leaves the lung unprotected so that neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar tissue and produces early emphysema. Only a proportion of PiZZ individuals develop clinically significant liver disease, reflecting modifying genetic and environmental factors.
additionalDifferentials: Biliary atresia and other causes of neonatal cholestasis
additionalInvestigations: Serum alpha-1-antitrypsin concentration, interpreted alongside acute-phase status
Phenotyping by isoelectric focusing and SERPINA1 genotyping
Liver biopsy with periodic acid-Schiff staining after diastase for characteristic globules
Liver ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging with alpha-fetoprotein for carcinoma surveillance
Pulmonary function tests and chest imaging to assess associated emphysema
Fibrosis assessment such as elastography and synthetic liver function tests
redFlags: Features of decompensated cirrhosis such as ascites, encephalopathy, or variceal bleeding
A new hepatic mass or rising alpha-fetoprotein suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma
Prolonged neonatal conjugated jaundice with failure to thrive
Rapidly progressive breathlessness indicating advancing emphysema
reference.prognosis: The liver phenotype is highly variable: many PiZZ individuals never develop significant hepatic disease, while others progress to cirrhosis in childhood or adulthood with a raised risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Avoidance of smoking and alcohol, and liver transplantation for end-stage disease, substantially improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Interpreting a normal alpha-1-antitrypsin level during acute inflammation as excluding the diagnosis
Overlooking the disorder as a cause of otherwise unexplained neonatal cholestasis or adult cirrhosis
Attributing liver disease solely to enzyme deficiency rather than to toxic hepatic protein accumulation
Failing to advise strict smoking and alcohol avoidance to protect lung and liver
Neglecting family screening and genetic counselling for a codominant inherited condition
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
